newsitem.title: UK: LME copper volatile ahead of expected stocks drop.
newsitem.headline: LME copper volatile ahead of expected stocks drop.

text.p: Copper prices whipsawed on the London Metal Exchange on Thursday afternoon ahead of another expected fall in inventories.
The other metals showed independence from the market leader as aluminium scored healthy gains and lead dipped to fresh lows.

The three month copper market slid in early afternoon trading to a low of $1,902 per tonne on speculative selling, echoing an overnight dive, after touching a morning high of $1,930 on news that workers at Kennecott's Utah operations went on strike.
The copper production plants were operating at a reduced level after 1,800 unionised workers walked off the job, a Kennecott spokeswoman said.
Prices finished the afternoon kerb towards the top of the range at $1,924, up $9.
Traders said stocks were expected to fall on Friday by 8,000-10,000 tonnes after declining by 10,950 tonnes on Tuesday.
"Stocks should keep falling for at least the next two dates. I've seen more warrant sales this week, but they won't show up until next week," one floor trader said.
"It's very difficult to get material out of Rotterdam and Antwerp and Italy is starting to get very tight also. Liverpool is nearly impossible," the trader added.
Another trader agreed that stocks draws were likely to continue, but the amounts would probably diminish.
The market is uncertain about how much of the stock erosion is going to meet end user demand and how much is being merely shifted around to bolster prices.
The premium of cash metal over three months metal rose during the afternoon, last traded at $15, compared to around $10 on Wednesday, and last bid at $20.

Aluminium made sharp gains during the day, which got a boost when stops were hit between $1,355 and $1,360, a floor trader said. Frantic buying in the last minutes of the kerb left the last trade at its high of $1,369, up $27.
The rally coincided with news that Russian President Boris Yeltsin sacked his security chief Alexander Lebed, but floor traders said the two were probably not connected.
Lead moved the opposite way, sinking to a fresh seven month low. It ended the kerb at $732, down $9 and just $1 above the low touched in March.
The next significant chart level was pegged at $715, the low hit on January 30, 1996.
Tin and zinc were only slightly weaker but held within ranges. Tin finished at $5,955, down $5 and zinc at $1,018, also off $5.
Nickel held at slightly stronger levels carved out earlier, with last kerb business at $7,080, up $15.
Alloy strengthened with the primary market, ending the day at $1,240, up from $1,225/28.
